checks.claim: Key: every sugar maple in the forest is a population (all individuals of one species in one area at one time)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'assemblages of organisms of a single species occupying the same geographic area at the same time'; OpenStax uses the same shape of example: 'a forest may include many pine trees, which represent the population of pine trees in this forest' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/1-2-themes-and-concepts-of-biology).

checks.claim: Wrong: every tree of any kind is a population (it is several species, so several populations)
checks.note: OpenStax: 'all of the trees, flowers, insects, and other populations in a forest form the forest's community'.

checks.claim: Wrong: sugar maples and beeches together are a population (two species)
checks.note: Two or more species together are a community, not a population.

checks.claim: Wrong: one sugar maple and its own seedlings is the population (only a few members of it)
checks.note: The definition is ALL the individuals of the species in the area ('all the individuals of a species living within a specific area'); the stem asks about the forest's population, so a subset is not it.

checks.claim: Sugar maple, American beech and yellow birch grow together in mixed hardwood forests (with deer, ferns, mushrooms)
checks.note: Grokipedia: sugar maple forms 'mixed stands with American beech (Fagus grandifolia), yellow birch (Betula alleghaniensis), and American basswood' in northern hardwood forests. Black maple is sometimes merged with sugar maple, which does not affect the question.

checks.claim: Context: the sugar maples young and old make up one population; several species are several populations
Key: tadpoles count in the bullfrog population, since they are the same species
checks.note: A population is all individuals of one species in an area; Grokipedia's account of population traits includes 'age structure, which describes the proportion of individuals at different life stages', so the young count.

checks.claim: Wrong: count them only once they have grown legs
checks.note: Membership depends on species, not life stage or legs.

checks.claim: Wrong: no, since tadpoles are too young to breed
checks.note: Non-breeding young are still members; age structure counts every age class.

checks.claim: Wrong: no, since tadpoles breathe with gills like fish
checks.note: They do use gills ('gill-dependent respiration'), but they are larval bullfrogs, the same species, not fish.

checks.claim: Bullfrogs lay eggs in shallow water; tadpole stage lasts one to three years
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'clutches of 10,000 to 20,000 eggs in shallow waters'; the tadpole stage 'lasts 1-3 years depending on environmental factors such as temperature'.

checks.claim: Stem: 'Each spring' the bullfrogs lay their eggs
checks.note: Breeding 'spans February to October in southern latitudes and May to July in northern ranges', so late spring into summer in the north. 'Each spring' is an acceptable simplification; 'each spring and summer' would be exact if the lead wants it.

checks.claim: Context: ecologists track how many are at each stage of life; a tadpole breathes with gills but is a young frog, not a fish
checks.note: Tadpole: 'the aquatic larval stage of frogs and toads', with gills replaced by lungs at metamorphosis.

checks.claim: Key: a community is the higher level because it is made up of many populations
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'an assemblage of interacting populations of two or more species occupying a defined geographic area at a given time'; OpenStax: 'A community is the sum of populations inhabiting a particular area'.

checks.claim: Wrong: it is one part of a larger population (reversed nesting)
checks.note: Higher levels are composed of lower ones; populations sit inside communities.

checks.claim: Wrong: it adds the water, mud and rocks (that is the ecosystem)
checks.note: Community has a 'biotic focus, excluding abiotic components that characterize broader ecosystems'.

checks.claim: Wrong: it holds more members of a single species
checks.note: More members of one species is still a population.

checks.claim: Context: a pond holds bullfrogs, sunfish, cattails and algae; water, mud and rocks join at the ecosystem level
checks.note: Ecosystem: 'a biological community of interacting organisms and their surrounding physical environment'. Cattails grow in ponds (Grokipedia, Typha).

checks.claim: Key: sunlight belongs to the ecosystem but not the community
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Abiotic factors comprise sunlight, temperature, water availability, soil composition, and inorganic nutrients'; communities exclude abiotic components (https://grokipedia.com/page/Community_(ecology)).

checks.claim: Wrong: the bacteria in its mud (alive, so in both)
checks.note: Community members are 'plants, animals, fungi, and microbes'. Kesler's pond example: 'The mud is full of bacteria and worms' (https://keslerscience.com/teks-5.12a-biotic-abiotic-interactions?hsLang=en).

checks.claim: Wrong: the algae on its surface (alive)
checks.note: Algae are producers in ponds; living, so community members.

checks.claim: Wrong: the cattails at its edge (alive)
checks.note: Living plants of ponds and marshes.

checks.claim: Context: community is the living things alone; ecosystem adds nonliving surroundings such as sunlight, water and mud
checks.note: OpenStax: 'all the living things in a particular area together with the abiotic, nonliving parts of that environment'.

checks.claim: Key: all of Earth's ecosystems together form the biosphere, the highest level
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the global sum of all ecosystems on Earth'; OpenStax: 'the collection of all ecosystems'.

checks.claim: Wrong: atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere
checks.note: Gases, water and solid Earth respectively; none is the sum of ecosystems.

checks.claim: Stem: life on Earth reaches from microbes drifting about 10 km up in the air (as the upper limit)
checks.note: Microbes ARE found near 10 km (Grokipedia Biosphere), but the stem gives 10 km as the top of life's reach, and that is wrong. Balloon cryosamplers flown from Hyderabad recovered living bacteria from air at 20 to 41 km (ScienceDaily 2009; the earlier 2001 flight's isolates were published in FEMS Microbiology Letters). Wikipedia's Biosphere article says life exists 'at least 64 km (40 mi) high in the atmosphere', and a Rueppell's vulture has been recorded at 11,300 m (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biosphere). Fix: 'from microbes drifting tens of kilometres up in the air' or 'from living microbes found more than 30 kilometres up', or keep 10 km and drop the implied limit: 'Life on Earth is found from high in the air, where microbes drift 10 kilometres up and more, to the floor of...'.

checks.claim: Stem: the floor of the deepest ocean trench is nearly 11 km down, and life is found there
checks.note: Challenger Deep 'maximum verified depth' 10,935 m; amphipods, microbial mats and Moritella bacteria found there.

checks.claim: Context: the biosphere is the whole zone where life is found; atmosphere = air, hydrosphere = all water, geosphere = solid ground; living things reach into each
Key: no other world is known to have life (cautious wording)
checks.note: Grokipedia (as of Feb 2026): 'no extraterrestrial life - microbial, complex, or intelligent - has been verified'; Wikipedia Biosphere: 'No biospheres have been detected beyond Earth'. The 2025 Perseverance Sapphire Canyon sample is only a 'potential biosignature' and confirmation awaits sample return (https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-says-mars-rover-discovered-potential-biosignature-last-year/). 'Is known to have' and 'know of no' are cautious enough. Time-sensitive: retire or rewrite if life is ever confirmed elsewhere.

checks.claim: Wrong: no other world is known to have water
checks.note: 'The residual north polar cap is almost entirely water ice'.

checks.claim: Wrong: no other world is known to have an atmosphere
checks.note: Venus's atmosphere is 96.5% carbon dioxide; Mars has a thin CO2 atmosphere.

checks.claim: Wrong: no other world is known to have clouds
checks.note: Venus has 'a continuous, opaque deck' of sulfuric acid clouds about 48 to 70 km up.

checks.claim: Context: Mars has water ice at its poles; Mars and Venus have atmospheres; Venus is wrapped in thick clouds; no life found on either or anywhere beyond Earth
checks.note: The south cap is mostly CO2 ice on top but has a thicker water-ice deposit beneath, so 'water ice at its poles' holds for both. Venus phosphine claims remain disputed, not a finding of life.

checks.claim: Key: following a nitrogen loop between trees, decomposers and soil is ecosystem-level study
checks.note: Ecosystems are 'dynamic systems where biotic and abiotic components interact through energy flow and nutrient cycling'; OpenStax names 'nitrogen in the soil' as an abiotic part of an ecosystem.

checks.claim: Wrong: the community (living things only; the soil is left out)
checks.note: Community excludes abiotic components.

checks.claim: Wrong: the population (one species; the loop involves trees, fungi and bacteria)
Wrong: the biosphere (the stem limits the study to one forest)
checks.note: The biosphere is the sum of all ecosystems; one forest is one ecosystem.

checks.claim: Plants take nitrogen up through roots; fungi and bacteria decomposing leaves return it to the soil
checks.note: Plants assimilate nitrogen 'primarily through roots'; ammonification 'occurs during decomposition of biomass by heterotrophic bacteria and fungi'.

checks.claim: Context: the soil is 'a nonliving part'
checks.note: At this grade the convention is that 'The soil itself is abiotic (it's not alive), but it's full of biotic factors' (Kesler); OpenStax lists 'nitrogen in the soil' as abiotic. Fine as written. Optional sharper wording, since Q4 stresses that mud bacteria are alive: 'a nonliving part, the soil's minerals' or 'the nitrogen held in the soil'.

checks.claim: Key: the town's people belong to its community, as one population
checks.note: Grokipedia lists 'human populations, wildlife species, vegetation, and microorganisms' as the biotic components of an urban ecosystem; a community is all the populations of living things in an area (OpenStax), and Aronson et al. 2016 (Ecology) call humans 'the dominant species in urban settings' when studying urban biotic communities (https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/126840/1/Aronson_et_al-2016-Ecology.pdf).

checks.claim: Wrong: in its ecosystem but not its community
checks.note: People are living, so they are in the community, not only in the nonliving surroundings.

checks.claim: Wrong: outside its ecosystem, apart from nature
checks.note: Humans are biotic components of urban ecosystems.

checks.claim: Wrong: in a separate community of their own
checks.note: An ecological community holds 'two or more species'; one species alone is a population.

checks.claim: Context: roads, houses and soil join them in the ecosystem; everyday speech calls a town's people its community; to an ecologist one species alone is never a community
checks.note: Everyday sense: 'a social aggregation of individuals linked by recurrent interactions'. Ecological sense requires two or more species.

checks.claim: Key: the log's group (many species, a community) is at the higher level than the squirrels (one species, a population)
checks.note: Kesler: 'A whole community fits under one rotting log'; 'Two squirrels in one yard are one population'. Matches the community and population definitions (Grokipedia Community (ecology), Population ecology).

checks.claim: Wrong: the squirrels, since they cover more ground
checks.note: Area does not define the level; one species over any area is a population.

checks.claim: Wrong: the squirrels, since each is a larger animal
Wrong: neither, since each group is one population
checks.note: The log's group is several species, so a community.

checks.claim: Beetles, ants, pill bugs, fungi and a salamander live under rotting logs; eastern gray squirrel is one species of eastern forests
checks.note: Decaying wood hosts insects, fungi, bacteria; Kesler's log lists 'pill bugs, beetles, ants, fungi, and a salamander'. Eastern gray squirrel: 'a species of tree squirrel' of eastern North American hardwood forests (https://grokipedia.com/page/Eastern_gray_squirrel).

checks.claim: Context (and grade_note): 'a step up the levels adds more kinds of living things, not more land' as a general rule
checks.note: True only of the step from population to community. The step from organism to population adds more individuals of the SAME species, not more kinds (a population is one species); the step from community to ecosystem adds nonliving surroundings, not more kinds of living things; and the biosphere, all of Earth's ecosystems, does add ground. Kesler's own wording ('Each step up adds more variety') is loose here. Fix the context: 'for the step from population to community adds more kinds of living things, not more land.' Fix the grade_note the same way ('the step from population to community adds kinds of living things, not area').

unit_notes: Definitions checked against Grokipedia (Population ecology, Community (ecology), Ecosystem, Biosphere), OpenStax Biology 2e 1.2 and Kesler TEKS 6.12C; all four levels and the biosphere are stated correctly. Two errors: Q 89f15ef1c3's stem gives 10 km as the top of life's reach, but living microbes have been recovered from 41 km and a vulture recorded at 11.3 km; Q 14533a8d14's context turns 'population to community adds kinds' into a rule for every step, and it is false for organism to population and community to ecosystem. Q d283e1020c is time-sensitive: no life has been confirmed beyond Earth as of 2026 (the Perseverance sample is only a potential biosignature); its wording is cautious enough. Humans as members of ecological communities is supported by urban-ecology sources (Grokipedia Urban ecosystem; Aronson et al. 2016).
